opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the competitive pressure has created a kind of herd mentality. Everybody in Silicon Valley is working on essentially the same thing: scaling up large language models, adding more data, more compute, more reinforcement learning on top, and hoping that somehow this will get us to human-level intelligence. And the reason is partly that nobody can afford to fall behind on the thing that's currently producing products and revenue. If your competitor ships a better chatbot next quarter, your investors want to know why you didn't.

That's understandable from a business point of view. LLMs are useful, there's no question about it. But I've been saying for a while that this is not the path to systems that really understand the physical world, that have persistent memory, that can reason and plan in a hierarchical way. A four-year-old has seen more data through vision than the biggest LLM has seen through text, and that child understands intuitive physics, object permanence, causality, things LLMs simply don't have. You're not going to get there by predicting the next token.

So the danger is that the competitive dynamics crowd out the longer-term research. When everyone is racing on the same track, the people who want to work on something different, like world models, joint embedding predictive architectures, learning from video and interaction, have a harder time getting resources inside those companies. And companies have also become much more closed. They used to publish everything; now a lot of them don't, because they think they have a secret sauce. I think that's a mistake. Progress in AI has always come from open research and from the community building on each other's ideas. Nobody has a monopoly on good ideas.

That's why I've been such a strong advocate of open source and open research. It's the best antidote to this kind of short-term, winner-take-all thinking. And honestly, I think the next big breakthroughs are probably going to come from people who aren't caught up in the LLM race, whether that's in academia, in smaller labs, or in places outside Silicon Valley entirely.

r001.rationale: It says companies follow the same LLM scaling path because nobody can afford to fall behind competitors and investors expect an answer if a rival ships a better chatbot.

r002.rationale: It mentions work outside Silicon Valley but does not say LeCun deliberately chose Paris for AMI Labs’ headquarters to avoid herd behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think competition has mostly been a good thing, actually. It accelerates progress, and it forces companies to actually ship things rather than sit on results. But there's a particular dynamic in Silicon Valley right now that I find a bit distorting, and it has to do with the concentration of money and attention on one paradigm.

Right now the dominant idea is that if you take a large language model and make it bigger, train it on more data, add more compute, you will eventually get to human-level intelligence. I don't believe that. I've said this many times. LLMs are useful, I use them, but they are fundamentally limited. They manipulate text, they don't understand the physical world, they have no persistent memory, they can't really reason or plan in any deep sense. And yet because they are commercially successful, almost all the capital in the industry is flowing in that direction.

So the incentive is to be a little bit better on the next benchmark, to release the next version a few months ahead of your competitor. That's a very short-horizon game. It pushes people toward incremental engineering rather than asking the harder question, which is: what is missing from these systems? Nobody wants to spend five years on an architecture that might not work when the board is asking why you don't have a chatbot as good as the other company's chatbot.

The other effect, which worries me more, is the move toward secrecy. For most of the history of AI, progress came from open research, people publishing, sharing code, building on each other's ideas. The transformer came out of a paper. ResNets, convolutional nets, all of this was published. Now some of the leading labs have essentially stopped publishing, because they view their methods as competitive advantage. I think that slows everyone down, including them, and it concentrates power in a way that is not healthy.

That's why I have been such a strong advocate of open platforms. If AI is going to become the infrastructure through which people access information, that infrastructure cannot be controlled by two or three companies on the West Coast of the United States. You need a diversity of systems, trained by many actors, reflecting many languages and cultures and value systems. Open-source models make that possible, and I think that is a much healthier equilibrium than the closed race we see today.

So to summarize: competition is good for speed, but the particular shape of the competition right now, one paradigm, closed research, short time horizons, is not necessarily good for getting to the next big ideas. Those will come from the people who are willing to step off the main road.

r001.rationale: The candidate says companies compete to release the next version ahead of rivals, and that this short-horizon incentive pushes them toward incremental work on the dominant LLM paradigm.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention Paris, AMI Labs, or a headquarters choice tied to avoiding Silicon Valley’s herd behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think competitive pressure creates a certain convergence. Once one company demonstrates that something works and there is a market for it, everybody else has a strong incentive to pursue the same thing. You get a lot of effort going into making similar systems better, faster, and cheaper.

That can produce very rapid progress. But it also makes it harder to pursue ideas that might take several years to work, particularly if they require questioning the approach that is currently making money. A startup has investors, a limited runway, and customers asking for features. Even a large company has pressure to respond to its competitors.

So you need room for research where the objective is not to match the next product release. Researchers need to be able to say: perhaps we are missing something fundamental, and we should investigate a different direction. Competition is very good at accelerating an approach once it works. It doesn't automatically ensure that we are exploring enough different approaches.

r001.rationale: The response says competitive pressure and the need to respond to competitors lead companies to pursue the same proven approach, capturing the incentive to avoid falling behind.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention LeCun choosing Paris for AMI Labs’ headquarters or connect that choice to avoiding Silicon Valley herd behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think competitive pressure creates a kind of convergence. If one company has a successful product, everyone else feels they need something comparable. So you get a lot of effort concentrated on language models, on assistants, on improving essentially the same set of capabilities. These are useful things, but commercial competition doesn’t necessarily produce diversity in research directions.

There’s a tension between doing research whose payoff might be five or ten years away and shipping something that keeps you competitive next quarter. If you believe there are fundamental limitations in the current approach, you have to be willing to work on alternatives even while the market is telling you to build a better version of what already sells.

That’s why I think it’s important to preserve room for long-term research, and for open research. You want people exploring different ideas, sharing results, and challenging the assumptions everybody else is making. Otherwise, you can have very intense competition and still have everyone running in the same direction.

r001.rationale: The response says competitive pressure makes companies converge: when one succeeds, others pursue comparable products and concentrate effort on the same capabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not mention AMI Labs, Paris, or LeCun choosing its headquarters to avoid Silicon Valley’s herd behavior.
